ba6c1da0793a1061.text: Spot the Scam. How not to get played by a dodgy text.

fd47165bacca7674.text: Your phone buzzes. Hi Mum, I dropped my phone. This is my new number. Can you help me pay a bill today? It looks normal. But it is a trap.

b821674bb8b32be3.text: In just seven months of 2022, more than one thousand one hundred Australians fell for this exact scam. They lost two point six million dollars.

5367d701e79dd0f1.text: Here's the secret. Scammers are writers. Every scam has a purpose: to get your money, your information, or your click. And every scam has an audience. You.

8efb10b1cec912b0.text: Red flag one. Rush. Pay today. Only two hours left. They rush you so you don't stop and think.

9bf80065da92cd4b.text: Red flag two. Reaction. They try to make you feel something big. Scared. Excited. Or sorry for someone.

c62e716e081832a1.text: Red flag three. Request. They ask you for money, a code, a password, or to click a link.

5e65f7aae02124ad.text: Red flag four. Random. An unknown number. A weird link. They don't use your name. Something just feels off.

0ed0480f1b1dcb3b.text: Spot a red flag? Stop. Don't click, pay or reply. Check. Contact the person or company using a number you already trust. Protect. Block it, report it, and tell someone.

346ae4b36ef6eee6.text: Your mission. Grab your workbook. Find the red flags. Then protect someone you care about.

c0af39007d0b8118.text: purpose. the reason a text was written — what the writer wants.

1c2da1c3fc1b454d.text: audience. the person or people a text is written for.

b1fd503d7bf1a374.text: Scammers are writers. Every message is written by someone, for a reason. A text from your coach tells you about training. An ad wants you to buy. A scam wants to trick you. Scammers think about who will read the message. They think about what they want you to do. Then they pick words to make you act fast. Most scams use 4 red flags: Rush — “Do it now!” Reaction — They make you scared, excited or sad. Request — They want money, a code or a click. Random — Something is odd. A number you don’t know. A strange link. Two or more red flags? Watch out. What should you do? Stop. Check. Protect. Don’t reply. Check with the real person or company. Use a number you already have. Then block it and tell someone.

68a66f8fc671edc9.text: The “Hi Mum” scam. In 2022, lots of people in Australia got a text: “Hi Mum, I lost my phone. This is my new number.” Then the “child” asked for money. It was a scam. The ACCC is a government group that protects shoppers. It said that in 7 months of 2022, more than 1,150 people were tricked. They lost $2.6 million. Most of them were parents and grandparents over 55. They loved their kids and wanted to help fast. The ACCC says: if you get a text from a new number, call the person on the number you already have. Think about it. Who did this scam trick? Which red flags can you find?

9a7d8208f2ea72a5.text: “Earn $500 a day liking videos”. Some scams look like a job. A message says: “Earn $500 a day liking videos!” At first they might pay you a little. Then they ask you to pay money to earn more. That money is gone. These scams trick people who want work — like young people looking for a first job. A real job never asks you to pay to start. Think about it. What is the purpose of this message? Why would a scammer pay you a little bit first?

674278ba07d6d537.text: Scammers are writers. Every message you get was written by someone, for a reason. A text from your coach tells you when training is on. An ad tries to make you buy something. A scam tries to trick you. Scammers are good writers. They think hard about who will read the message (the audience) and what they want the reader to do (the purpose). Then they choose words that push you to act fast. Most scams use the same four tricks. We call them the 4 red flags: Rush — “Act now!” “Last chance!” They don’t want you to have time to think. Reaction — They make you feel scared, excited or sorry for someone. Big feelings switch off careful thinking. Request — They want something: money, a gift card, a code, your password, or a click. Random — Something doesn’t fit. A number you don’t know. A strange link. Spelling that’s a bit off. They don’t use your name. One red flag doesn’t always mean scam. Your mate might really be in a rush! But two or more red flags is a big warning. The best move? Stop. Check. Protect. Don’t reply to the message. Check by contacting the person or company another way — use a number or app you already have, not the one in the message. Then block, report and tell someone.

81aadc57eb771605.text: The “Hi Mum” scam. In 2022, a scam message spread across Australia. It went like this: “Hi Mum, I’ve lost my phone. This is my new number.” After a few friendly messages, the “child” asked for money to pay an urgent bill. The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) said that in the first seven months of 2022, more than 1,150 Australians fell for it and lost $2.6 million. Most of the reports came in June and July. Most people who were tricked were parents and grandparents over 55. The scammers knew their audience: people who love their kids and want to help them fast. The ACCC’s advice: if you get a message from a number you don’t know, check by calling the person on the number you already have for them. Think about it. Who was the audience for this scam? Which red flags can you find in “Hi Mum, I’ve lost my phone”? Why do you think it worked so well on parents?

cbe1cb793fa63210.text: “Earn $500 a day liking videos”. Scamwatch warns about fake job offers sent by text, WhatsApp and social media. They promise easy money for simple tasks, like liking videos or rating products. At first, they might even pay you a little bit — so it feels real. Then they ask you to pay money to “unlock” bigger earnings. That money is gone. These scams target people who want work — including young people looking for their first job. Real jobs never ask you to pay to start. Think about it. What is the purpose of this message? Why would a scammer pay you a little bit first?

358a60ce63b95edd.text: Who were most of the people tricked by the ‘Hi Mum’ scam? Is it: Teenagers? Or People over 55? Or Gamers? Or Business owners?

A scam tries to trick you. Scammers are good writers. They think hard about who will read the message (the audience) and what they want the reader to do (the purpose). Then they choose words that push you to act fast. Most scams use the same four tricks. We call them the 4 red flags: Rush — “Act now!” “Last chance!” They don’t want you to have time to think. Reaction — They make you feel scared, excited or sorry for someone. Big feelings switch off careful thinking. Request — They want something: money, a gift card, a code, your password, or a click. Random — Something doesn’t fit. A number you don’t know. A strange link. Spelling that’s a bit off. They don’t use your name. One red flag doesn’t always mean scam. Check by contacting the person or company another way — use a number or app you already have, not the one in the message. Then block, report and tell someone. Why it works. Scammers use the same techniques as advertisers: urgency, emotive language and a clear call to action. Some scams copy the logo, layout and tone of real companies so the message looks credible. Reading critically means asking not just what a message says, but how it is trying to position you — and who benefits if you do what it asks.
